strengths: The shared treatment of forest leaf partitions and ReLU activation regions offers an interesting approach to confidence estimation without OOD training examples. Researchers working on uncertainty estimation for tabular and vision models have an identifiable reason to study it.

The experimental coverage includes six simulation families, 45 OpenML datasets, and vision benchmarks. Known-posterior simulations, 45 simulation repetitions, comparisons of Euclidean and partition-based distances, and per-dataset appendix plots provide useful evidence.

The reported results suggest a useful accuracy–calibration tradeoff: on CIFAR-10, KDN reduces MCE from 0.09 to 0.04 while accuracy changes from 77.78% to 76.84%. Several simulations also show improved posterior estimation relative to the parent models.

For a fixed fitted model, positive density floor, and finite positive Gaussian bandwidths, the prior-reversion mechanism in Proposition 4 is sound when distance is interpreted in the Gaussian feature space.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the probabilistic formulation. Equation (3) identifies discriminative outputs with class-conditional densities, although ReLU logits are not densities and forest class probabilities estimate posteriors. Furthermore, the nearest-kernel selector in Equations (5) and (13) generally discards probability mass, and adding b/log(n) over R^d makes the resulting function nonintegrable. Equation (7) still defines normalized confidence scores, but its claimed Bayes-density interpretation is unsupported. A consistent score-based interpretation or a properly normalized probabilistic model is needed.

Necessary: Distinguish prior reversion from calibration. Low marginal density does not imply that the true conditional label distribution equals the training prior, as prescribed by Equation (1). Proposition 4 establishes a limit at infinite distance, not calibrated predictions throughout the OOD region; for the vision model, distance in encoder space also need not track distance in input space. OCE measures agreement of maximum confidence with the maximum prior, rather than calibration against outcomes, and under class imbalance it does not even establish agreement of the full probability vectors. The claims should be narrowed accordingly. Expanding-hypersphere experiments support remote-input confidence reduction but provide limited evidence about other distribution shifts.

Necessary: Resolve discrepancies that prevent faithful implementation. Equations (9)–(10) estimate Gaussian parameters from samples within each polytope, whereas Algorithm 1 specifies weighted maximum likelihood using cross-polytope weights. Algorithms 2–3 return the raw similarity without the exponentiation in Equation (15). The value or selection procedure for b, the search grid and objective for k, and handling of ties in nearest-polytope selection are unspecified. These choices directly affect the reported ID–OOD tradeoff; promised code release after acceptance does not resolve the current ambiguity.

Necessary: Clarify and audit the experimental statistics and baseline protocols. Section 5 describes FPR@95 as fixing precision, whereas the conventional metric fixes true-positive rate. Table 1 reports KDN AUROC of 1.00 alongside FPR@95 of 0.14 on SVHN and 0.12 on noise; these combinations require explanation under the actual metric definition. Specify score orientation, threshold selection, repetitions, and the meaning of the reported uncertainties, together with OOD baseline training data and tuning procedures. Comparative claims also need qualification: for example, CIFAR-100 OCE is 0.20 for KDN versus 0.01 for OE.

Optional improvements: Ablations of the additive floor, similarity weighting, and nearest-kernel selection would clarify which components produce the gains. A simple density-based comparator using the same representation would also be informative. Runtime and memory measurements would help readers assess the stated quadratic training cost.
